A transthoracic echocardiogram is recommended to identify structural heart disease in newly detected LBBB C.

Cardiac resynchronization therapy is recommended for patients with left bundle branch block (LBBB) who have depressed systolic function, heart failure symptoms, and a QRS duration of greater than 120 msecond after optimal heart failure therapy. A

Cardiac resynchronization therapy significantly reduces worsening of heart failure and improves quality of life and exercise tolerance in patients with chronic heart failure and intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD). B

background.definition: Conduction disturbances occurring at various levels of the branches of the His-Purkinje system are defined as bundle branch blocks or intraventricular conduction delays (IVCDs).

list.listitem: The overall prevalence of BBB in men increases with age from 1% at age 50 years to 17% at age 80 years leading to a cumulative incidence of 18% (left BBB = 6.5%; right BBB = 12.9%) .
Depending on the sampling criteria used, the prevalence of LBBB in the general population is estimated to range from 0.1 – 0.8% .
In an Icelandic population, the general incidence of LBBB was 3.2 per 10, 000 per year for men and 3.7 per 10,000 for women .
In the Copenhagen heart study, the prevalence of RBBB was 1.4% in men and 0.5% in women, while the prevalence of incomplete RBBB was 4.7% and 2.3% in men and women respectively .
The incidence of RBBB from a study done in Spain was around 0.8% per year, including both complete RBBB and incomplete RBBB .

The causes of bundle branch block can be classified into cardiac, pulmonary, procedure-related, and other causes. Cardiac causes can be broken down into myocardial, valvular, and electrical or conduction system causes
Left ventricular hypertrophy due to hypertension
Ischemic heart disease or myocardial infarction (MI)
Infiltrative diseases (sarcoidosis, amyloidosis)
Cardiomyopathy (ischemic or dilated)
Inflammatory diseases like myocarditis and endocarditis.
Congenital heart diseases (eg, Ebstein's anomaly, atrial septal defect)
Aortic and mitral valvular heart disease
Idiopathic progressive cardiac conduction diseases such as Lev's disease or Lenègre's disease.
Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern (accessory pathway)
BBB may be functional, as in rate-related bundle branch block which is a result of a long preceding R-R interval followed by a short cycle .
Pulmonary causes can be further divided into airway, lung parenchyma, pulmonary vessels, and pleural causes
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
Acute Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH)
Diffuse Parenchymal Lung Diseases (DPLD)
Pneumothorax
Closure of ventral septal defects
Right heart catheterization
Nonsurgical septal reduction therapy with ethanol ablation
Post-transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR)
Post-septal myectomy/myotomy
Neuromuscular diseases like muscular dystrophy
Drug toxicity such as digitalis.
Electrolyte abnormality such as hyperkalemia.

Normally, the cardiac electrical impulse is conducted from the sinus node to the bundle of His through the atrioventricular node. It then travels down the left and right bundles and terminates in the Purkinje fibers spreading to the ventricular muscles.
BBB results from a conduction delay and/or damage to the bundle of His or its branches that constitute the intraventricular conduction system from any cardiac or pulmonary cause as mentioned above.
BBB can be chronic or intermittent; complete or incomplete.
Delayed conduction in bundle branches results in asynchronous activation of ventricular sites, which leads to characteristic electrocardiographic patterns.

LBBB causes the right ventricle to be activated first, followed by the left ventricular (LV) endocardium. The rest of the LV is activated in a delayed fashion with the lateral basal area being the last to be activated. This activation sequence leads to dyssynchronous motion of the ventricular walls extending isovolumic contraction and relaxation times, resulting in decreased contraction efficiency.

Delay or blockage in the right bundle branch system results in the initial activation of the left side of ventricular septum. This spreads transeptally to the right side of the ventricular septum and then to the right ventricular anterior free wall, lateral right ventricular wall, and finally the right ventricular outflow tract.
Despite this delay in conduction, RBBB is associated with less ventricular dyssynchrony as compared to LBBB .
Patients often present incidentally or during investigation for cardiovascular symptoms such as dizziness, palpitations, or syncope. C
12-lead ECG establishes the diagnosis of BBB. C
Consider cardiac imaging when there is a concern for structural heart disease C.
Consider electrophysiology study in patients where the cause of symptoms has not been established and ECG data are non diagnostic. C
Electrophysiology study is not recommended in asymptomatic patients with IVCD or symptomatic patients whose symptoms can be correlated with ECG events. C

The diagnostic criteria for the different types of bundle branch blocks according to the 2018 American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) guideline is shown in Table 1 .
The mnemonic ‘WiL LiaM MuRRoW’ can aid in the identification of these patterns on an EKG as shown in figure 1.
WiL LiaM for LBBB with the first letter W representing the QRS wave in lead V1 and M representing the QRS in leads V5 or V6.
In LBBB, there is a small initial r wave, rS or QS wave in leads V1-V3 and broad notched R wave or RS wave in lateral leads V5, V6, I and aVL.
Similarly, MuRRoW for RBBB the first letter M representing the QRS wave in lead V1 and W representing the QRS in lead V5 or V6.
In RBBB, there is a rsr', rsR' or rSR' pattern of the QRS wave in leads V1 or V2 and deep S wave with longer duration than R (>40 ms) in the left precordial leads V5 and V6..
Patients may be asymptomatic or may present with palpitations, dizziness, fatigue, chest pain, presyncope, syncope, or sudden death, all of which may depend on their co-morbidities

They may be of advanced age or may have a history of pulmonary disease, congenital heart disease, myocardial infarction, structural heart disease, family history of sudden death, or may have a history of cardiac surgery

Syncope in patients with BBB is associated with an increased risk of mortality and other cardiac events if they are of an advanced age. This is due to the increased likelihood of the presence of underlying heart disease .

On physical examination, with RBBB there may be wide splitting of the second heart sound due to delayed closure of the pulmonic valve, whereas in LBBB paradoxical splitting may occur due to delayed closure of the aortic valve .
The rest of the physical examination depends on the associated cardiopulmonary co-morbidities.
Recommendations for evaluating patients with BBB were published in the ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 guidelines on bradycardia and cardiac conduction delay as shown in figure 2 .
A resting 12-lead electrocardiogram remains the cornerstone diagnostic test for BBB. ECG diagnostic criteria as recommended by the 2018 ACC/AHA guideline on bradycardia are shown in Table 1.
An ambulatory ECG should be considered in patients with paroxysmal symptoms and an inconclusive resting ECG. This may help establish a symptom - rhythm relationship.
When a structural heart disease is suspected as the etiology of the block, a 2-dimensional echocardiogram (2D ECHO) is recommended.

If the 2D ECHO is inconclusive for a structural heart disease, then advanced imaging such as a cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, and nuclear studies should be considered if suspicion remains high particularly.
Electrophysiologic study (EPS) should be considered when symptoms are suggestive of intermittent bradycardia with no identifiable abnormality on ECG.

Electrophysiologic evaluation of IVCD also includes evaluation of AV node, sinus node, and programmed atrial and ventricular stimulation to assess for development of any tachyarrhythmias or bradyarrhythmia's because sudden death in patients with bifascicular block may not be caused by complete Tri fascicular block but by ventricular tachyarrhythmias .
In patients who develop LBBB following transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), an EPS can be used to identify those at risk of developing a high atrioventricular block .
Stress testing should be considered in patients with LBBB without symptoms, who are clinically suspected of having ischemic heart disease.
BBB is often discovered incidentally, or may be found as the result of the investigation of cardiovascular symptoms such as syncope, palpitations, or dizziness.
ECG is the best initial test for BBB, followed by Holter monitor or event monitor for paroxysmal symptoms, and electrophysiologic studies if symptoms remain undiagnosed.
Based on the 2018 recommendations by ACC/AHA, indications for permanent pacing in patients with BBB are as shown in the figure 3.
A permanent pacemaker is recommended for patients with alternating bundle branch block and in symptomatic BBB with His-Ventricular interval > 70 msec C .
Cardiac resynchronization therapy is recommended for patients with systolic heart failure with an ejection fraction lesser than 35% and QRS greater than 120 msec after optimal medical therapy A.
Patients with dilated cardiomyopathy and acceleration-dependent LBBB may benefit from restoration of a narrow QRS complex by suppressing the heart rate with beta blockers.
A permanent pacemaker is recommended for patients with alternating bundle branch block and in symptomatic BBB with His-Ventricular interval > 70 msec .

Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) is indicated for patients who have LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB with a QRS duration ≥150 ms, and NYHA class II, III, or ambulatory IV symptoms despite optimal medical therapy .
CRT is useful in patients with LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB with a QRS duration of 120 to 149 ms, and NYHA class II, III, or ambulatory IV symptoms on goal directed medical therapy .
CRT may be considered for patients who have LVEF ≤30%, ischemic cause of HF, sinus rhythm, LBBB with a QRS duration ≥150 ms, and NYHA class I symptoms on optimal medical therapy .

An individual patient level meta-analysis (n=6264) found a lower risk of hospitalization for heart failure or death in patients with a QRS interval >= 150 ms and either LBBB (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.48-0.66) or intraventricular conduction delay (HR 0.59, 95% 0.39-0.89). No benefit was found for patients with RBBB.
In acute emergency, temporary pacing via transcutaneous or transvenous route should be done until BBB resolves or as a bridge to permanent cardiac pacemakers.
A temporary pacemaker may be used in patients with isolated LBBB who are undergoing right-sided cardiac catheterization because of the potential for transient complete heart block. .
Correct electrolyte abnormalities.
Treat infectious causes such as endocarditis.
Treat underlying lung diseases such as acute pulmonary embolism and pneumothorax.
Avoid drugs that prolong AV node conduction.
Hospitalize patients with symptomatic BBB to confirm the diagnosis.
Refer patients to determine reversible causes, such as myocardial ischemia.
Refer patients to determine the need for electrophysiology study and pacemaker placement.
Refer patients who meet the criteria for cardiac resynchronization therapy.
Syncope; pacemaker implantation.

LBBB induced cardiomyopathy: Among this population left bundle branch pacing is a reasonable option for CRT due to the reported complete correction of the underlying electrical and mechanical abnormalities following this procedure .

Painful LBBB syndrome: Left bundle branch area pacing and permanent His bundle branch pacing are two different approaches to pacing that have been reported in the successful management of painful LBBB syndrome .
Complete RBBB and LBBB are independent predictors of all-cause mortality risk. A
Cardiac resynchronization therapy slows worsening of heart failure and improves quality of life and exercise tolerance in patients with chronic heart failure and IVCD. B
In a retrospective US study, the risk of progression of LBBB to complete atrioventricular block was approximately 1% per year .
Although LBBB may be relatively benign in younger patients, it serves as an important risk factor for cardiovascular disease in older patients.
LBBB has been reported as a predictor of sudden cardiac death (10-fold incidence increase) and myocardial infarction (2.90 x increased risk) particularly among individuals aged 50 years and older .

In a retrospective US study, LBBB was reportedly associated with an increased risk of worsening systolic heart failure (HR: 1.34; 95% CU: 1.09 – 1.63) and implantable cardioverter-defibrillator device placement (HR: 1.50; 95% CI 1.10 – 2.10) .

In transcutaneous aortic valve implantation (TAVI) populations, TAVR-induced LBBB was shown to correlate with an increased rate of a new pacemaker implantation during hospitalization and at 1-year follow up according to reports from the Placement of Aortic Transcatheter Valves (PARTNER) trial .

Conventionally, in the absence of cardiovascular diseases, RBBB was not associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes. This is supported by findings from earlier studies such as the Heart Outcomes Prevention Evaluation (HOPE) trial and the Women Health Initiative study .

However, in recent times, studies have reported that RBBB in the absence of cardiovascular disease is associated with an increase in all-cause (HR, 1.5; 95% CI 1.1 - 2.0) and cardiovascular-related mortality (HR, 1.7; 95% CI, 1.1 - 2.8) .
When compared to those without RBBB, RBBB was shown to increase the risk of in-hospital mortality (8.64% vs 3.74%, p = 0.034) in patients with acute myocardial infarction .
RBBB has also been associated with an adverse prognosis among patients with heart failure .

Biventricular pacing or cardiac resynchronization therapy significantly reduces worsening of heart failure and improves exercise tolerance and quality of life in patients with chronic heart failure and IVCD.
Data from two large US registries show an excess of mortality in patients with RBBB treated with CRT .
Perform close follow up as clinically indicated in patients with structural heart disease and bifascicular block to look for progression of block and possible need for pacemaker implantation.
Pacemaker function should be assessed before discharge after pacemaker implantation.
Perform periodic telephonic monitoring with intermittent clinic evaluation to assess pacemaker function.
For patients with a dual-chamber pacemaker, perform clinic follow up twice in the first 6 months and then once every 6 months.

Clinic follow up includes assessment of the clinical status of the patient, battery status, pacing threshold, pulse width, sensing function, lead integrity, and optimization of sensor-driven rate response.

In a retrospective study of patients with LBBB who underwent a myocardial perfusion test, regadenoson stress SPECT-MPI provided an independent prognostic value of predicting adverse cardiac events, with an annualized major adverse cardiovascular event rate of 0.8% .
Avoid AV blocking medications.
In case of any symptoms, follow up with clinic immediately.
Permanent pacemaker may be indicated in children with transient postoperative third-degree AV block that reverts to sinus rhythm with residual bifascicular block.TAVI populations
Careful surveillance for bradycardia is reasonable in patients with new persistent bundle branch block following TAVI .

TAVR candidates with pre-existing RBBB may benefit from selective prophylactic permanent pacemaker implantation due to its possible impact on TAVR procedural time, length of hospital stay, and cardiac rehospitalization .
